newsitem.title: GERMANY: Siemens ANL seeks net rates.
newsitem.headline: Siemens ANL seeks net rates.

text.p: Siemens AG Industrial & Building Systems (ANL) said it is moving towards net freight rates deals with transport carriers and fixed fee payments for freight forwarders.

Steffen Rudkowsky, Siemens ANL traffic and shipping manager, said the company wanted tight logistics control over its freight including a veto on carriers but did not plan extensive direct purchasing from suppliers.

"We bring in logistics know-how to define the catalogue of requirements for the forwarder or shipping company as exactly as possible, to fix the interfaces and to decide who does which part," he said in a Reuters interview.
Siemens already had a good overview of market rates but did not want to press rates down at the cost of service and quality, he added.
"The rates which are offered on the market to the forwarders are also known to us. We can very easily judge whether a forwarder brings out a market-orientated, low price," he said.
But Rudkowsky stressed: "Value-for-money purchasing yes but never so low that the quality of the service suffers as a result."
Examples of net carrier rate and fixed forwarder fee agreements were the current contract with Hansa Meyer for Indonesia and with MSAS Cargo International last year, he said.
In both cases, air cargo capacity had been secured at a directly-negotiated rate with Lufthansa Cargo AG and the forwarding parter received separate payment from the shipper for its services.
MSAS organised the record-breaking transport of a 48.5 tonne electrical motor from Berlin to Canada last summer, which was the heaviest ever air cargo flown by Lufthansa Cargo.

"We agreed as partners that the forwarder would receive an appropriate sum for the services which he supplied, not on a kilo basis which would have cost us three or four times as much but a fair sum," Rudkowsky said.
But, in contrast to sister company Siemens KWU, Siemens ANL had only rarely bought cargo space directly from carriers such as Lufthansa or Cargolux (CLUX.CN), he said.
Siemens often used specialised, medium-sized freight forwarders who were able to provide more individual service instead of the "mass business" of larger forwarders, he noted.
"The partner must offer all the options which we need for a particular project but then it makes no difference to me how big or small he is but the service must be right."

Rudkowsky said: "As far as the choice of carrier or shipping company is concerned, we always have an absolute right to co-decide. We always have a right of veto or approval to say which airline or shipping company is to be used."
Siemens ensured, for example, that it flew a sufficient proportion with Lufthansa Cargo since the German carrier supplied a large amount of air cargo space to the market.

"We need the Lufthansa capacity and so with certain loads or smaller consignments, when the conditions are right or it makes no difference, we ensure that the carrier also profits from this." --Reuters Air Cargo Newsroom. Tel +44 171 542 7706; Fax: 5017
